item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
For what it matters, I thought the log was well written and adds to the article. Callous indifference on the part of foundation personnel is what is being demonstrated.

Yes, it would be standard procedure for medical stuff performed on a woman to be done by a woman. They don't care enough to do that, though, because they are treating her like just another thing (which some ass tried to take advantage of). She got pissed and spoke out.

item.content:encoded:
The most efficient way I could see to do that is to remove this interview log and write three others, one for each member of the family. Was that what you had in mind?

One of the critiques I received initially was that the main body was very long (I've shortened it considerably), but I don't see a way to fit it in there anyway.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I don't think it worked out for me, due to the point I've addressed above. Regardless of the nature of the test, if it were medically related, it's more likely to be conducted by a female if the subject's a female.

To me, it shows a level of incompetency in the Foundation rather than opening up the window of humanisation.

Instead, you can focus directly on how they (as in, all 4 of them) feel about being a plaything for the Foundation and flesh out each of the 4 as individual characters. I've realised it's rather focused on -C, but what about the others?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I can see why it would be.

The idea behind the event itself was that taking fluid samples was not his reason for interacting with her. He was supposed to be performing a test of a different nature.

The idea behind having the event is to humanize her by making the reader sympathize for her. It opens up the opportunity for her to humanize the whole family.

Yes, it is jarring. There was at least some intent behind that.

Does that make sense? Does it not work?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
He tried to touch me.

He said it was to take fluid samples from my–

Uh… in real life, when one needs to perform medical procedures on women, it is usually a female who does it (for obvious reasons). I'm sure they could get a female employee to retrieve fluid samples from a female anomalous humanoid.

In any case, the plot point about a researcher behaving inappropriate at work to a test subject is jarring and not-all-that-logical.
